title: String Quintet in C major
hook: Schubert’s last chamber work, finished two months before he died and never heard in his lifetime.

painting.title: The Stages of Life
painting.pairingNote: Five figures on an evening shore and five ships coming in, painted in Friedrich’s last working years; like the quintet, a late work in which calm and farewell sit side by side.

facts: Schubert wrote the quintet in the late summer or early autumn of 1828, alongside his last three piano sonatas, and finished it about two months before his death in November, at the age of 31. He offered it to the publisher Probst, mentioning that it would soon be rehearsed; Probst asked instead for songs and easier piano music.

No performance in Schubert’s lifetime is known. The work waited until 17 November 1850 for its first known public performance, at the Musikverein in Vienna, and was published in 1853. The manuscript is lost.

Most string quintets of the time, including Mozart’s in C major, add a second viola to the string quartet. Schubert adds a second cello. The lower half of the group becomes rich and dark, and either cello can soar into a high, singing register while the other holds the bass.
It is long, almost an hour in this recording, and the first movement alone takes more than a third of it.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a vast, glowing opening (I), a still, timeless song with a storm at its heart (II), a fierce hunt with a frozen trio (III), a Hungarian-flavoured dance that ends on a jarring note (IV).

movements.heading: Allegro ma non troppo
movements.summary: The quintet opens not with a tune but with a single long chord that swells and then turns sour. From this slow beginning grows a huge [[sonata-form|sonata form]], full of sudden changes of key. Its heart is the second theme: a long, tender duet for the two cellos.

mainIdeas.name: The opening chord
mainIdeas.description: C major, held and swelling, then clouding over.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2
mainIdeas.description: a warm, lilting duet for the two cellos in E-flat major, over a soft accompaniment.

mainIdeas.name: The march
mainIdeas.description: a firm, dotted rhythm that closes the exposition and drives the development.

stops.hear: One long chord from all five, swelling, then darkening into a strange harmony
stops.happening: The opening: C major, with no clear tune or beat

stops.hear: The music gathers speed and tension; the instruments start to move faster
The two cellos sing a long, swaying duet in their high register; the others accompany softly
The same tune, now high in the first violin and viola
Firmer music with a strong, dotted, march-like rhythm
The long opening chord again
Instead of going home, the music slides quietly into a brighter, unexpected key
stops.happening: The [[development|development]] begins, moving from G major to A major

stops.hear: The opening chord returns, now decorated with quick rising figures
The cellos’ duet once more
The march rhythm and the opening idea, in a final, quieter summing-up

notice: Listen to the two cellos in the second theme. One plays the tune high, the other answers or doubles below: a sound no quartet can make.
Notice how often the key slips without warning, at the opening chord, at the start of the development. Schubert makes sudden changes of light his main drama.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The Melos Quartett with Mstislav Rostropovich as second cellist recorded the quintet in the Tonhalle, Zurich, in September 1977. They take the repeat of the first movement’s exposition (≈ 5:18), which is one reason the movement lasts over twenty minutes; the other is the slow, spacious tempo, especially in the Adagio.

movements.heading: Adagio
movements.summary: A very slow movement in three parts. The outer parts, in E major, are almost motionless: three instruments sustain a quiet hymn while the first violin and the second cello add short, separate notes. In the middle a storm breaks out in F minor. When the calm returns, it carries a memory of the storm.

mainIdeas.name: The hymn
mainIdeas.description: long, soft chords in the second violin, viola and first cello.

mainIdeas.name: The commentary
mainIdeas.description: little phrases in the first violin, and plucked notes in the second cello.

mainIdeas.name: The storm
mainIdeas.description: a passionate, sobbing melody over restless, throbbing accompaniment and trills, in F minor.

stops.hear: A slow, hushed hymn in the middle instruments; above, the violin drops in short phrases, and below, the second cello plucks single notes
stops.happening: The first section, in E major; the second cello plays [[pizzicato|pizzicato]]

stops.hear: Without warning, a loud outburst: trills, restless throbbing notes and a wailing tune high up
stops.happening: The middle section, in F minor

stops.hear: The storm subsides into soft, uncertain chords
The hymn returns, but the second cello now runs in quick, rippling notes beneath it
stops.happening: The first section, changed by the storm

stops.hear: In the last bars the harmony slides back towards F minor for a moment, then settles in E major
stops.happening: The storm’s key, remembered once more

notice: In the first minutes, listen to the three layers: the hymn in the middle, the violin’s fragments above, the plucked bass below.
After the storm, follow the second cello. Its quick runs are new: the calm music now has motion underneath it.

movements.heading: Scherzo. Presto – Trio. Andante sostenuto
movements.summary: A loud, full [[scherzo|scherzo]] like a hunting scene, using the open strings of the lower instruments to make a sound almost too big for five players. Its [[trio|trio]] is the opposite: slow, quiet and dark, in the distant key of D-flat major, before the scherzo returns.

mainIdeas.name: The scherzo
mainIdeas.description: a vigorous, stamping tune with horn-like calls, in C major.

mainIdeas.name: The trio
mainIdeas.description: a slow, hushed, almost motionless melody in D-flat major.

stops.hear: Loud, full, galloping music, like a hunt with horns
The tune is flung into distant keys, and back
stops.happening: Sudden changes of key, a Schubert hallmark

stops.hear: Everything stops. A slow, quiet melody begins, as if from another world
The loud hunting music again

stops.label: Last 20 seconds
stops.hear: A hard, emphatic close

notice: Listen to the moment the trio begins. The speed, the volume and the key all change at once, so that the music seems to freeze.

movements.heading: Allegretto
movements.summary: A lively finale with a dance-like main theme that has a Hungarian accent. It is a [[rondo|rondo]] in which the main tune keeps coming back, and its mood keeps swinging between major and minor. The ending speeds up, and the last two notes are a famous shock.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a swinging, accented dance, half in minor, half in major.

mainIdeas.name: The second theme
mainIdeas.description: a smoother, singing tune in the lower instruments.

stops.hear: A lively dance with strong accents and a Hungarian flavour; it seems unsure whether to be in major or minor
A gentler, singing tune
The dance tune again
The dance once more, after a stretch of new keys
The tempo picks up; the music races

stops.label: Last 10 seconds
stops.hear: Two final loud notes played together by everyone: one note that clashes, then C
stops.happening: The ending: D-flat, then C, in [[unison|unison]]

notice: Listen to the very last two notes. The first, D-flat, is a semitone away from the home note, and it grinds; only then comes C.

threads.title: Two cellos
threads.body: The extra cello makes the low register dark and full, and frees one cello to sing high. It shapes the first movement’s duet, the Adagio’s plucked bass and the scherzo’s huge sound.

threads.title: A semitone away
threads.body: E major against F minor in the Adagio, C major against D-flat in the scherzo, and D-flat to C in the last two notes: the same small step returns as the work’s biggest shock.

threads.title: Late Schubert
threads.body: Like the last piano sonatas written alongside it, the quintet is long, unhurried and full of sudden turns of light. Knowing that it was written months before his death, many listeners hear it as a farewell, though there is no sign that Schubert expected to die so soon.
